passages.t: A herdsman from Tekoa, and the LORD's roar
passages.happening:
‘These are the words of Amos, who was among the sheepherders of Tekoa’ (verse 1). They are what he saw concerning Israel two years before the earthquake, when Uzziah was king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Jehoash was king of Israel.

He said, ‘The LORD roars from Zion and raises His voice from Jerusalem’ (verse 2). The shepherds' pastures mourn, and the top of Carmel withers.
passages.hearers:
Tekoa was a village in the hills of Judah, about ten miles (sixteen kilometers) south of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness. The word for sheepherder is used elsewhere of King Mesha of Moab, who paid thousands of lambs in tribute, so Amos may have been a substantial breeder or manager of flocks rather than a poor hired hand; interpreters differ. Either way, he was not a prophet by trade, and he spoke in the northern kingdom as an outsider from Judah.

The heading places Amos in the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, and most date his preaching around 760 BC. The earthquake was remembered for centuries. Excavations at Hazor and other sites have found damage from a strong earthquake that archaeologists date to roughly the middle of the eighth century BC. Many connect it with this one, though the dating of such layers is approximate and the link is probable rather than certain.

Verse 2 is a motto for the whole book. The LORD roars like a lion, and the land dries up from the southern pastures to the top of Mount Carmel in the north.
passages.later: Centuries later Zechariah still spoke of people fleeing ‘from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah’ (Zechariah 14:5). Joel opens his last promise with the same words: ‘The LORD will roar from Zion and raise His voice from Jerusalem’ (Joel 3:16).
passages.asks: God called a herdsman, not a professional, to speak for him. Ask whether you have assumed that God speaks only through certain kinds of people. And ask what it would mean for you to hear the LORD's voice as a roar and not a whisper you can ignore.

passages.happening:
Each judgment begins with the same words, with a new name each time: ‘For three transgressions of Damascus, even four, I will not revoke My judgment’. Damascus is judged ‘because they threshed Gilead with sledges of iron’ (verse 3). God will send fire on the house of Hazael, break the gates of Damascus, and send Aram's people into exile to Kir (verses 4-5).

Gaza is judged ‘because they exiled a whole population, delivering them up to Edom’ (verse 6). Fire will burn its walls, and the rulers of Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron will be cut off (verses 7-8). Tyre is judged because ‘they delivered up a whole congregation of exiles to Edom and broke a covenant of brotherhood’ (verse 9), and fire will consume its citadels (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The three-then-four pattern is a common Hebrew way of saying that sin has piled up past the limit. Each judgment follows the same shape: the formula, a specific charge, fire on walls and citadels. The repetition builds, and it lulls the hearer into agreement.

These nations were real powers with real histories of war against Israel. Damascus was the capital of Aram. Its kings Hazael and Ben-hadad had laid waste Israel's land east of the Jordan in the late ninth century. Threshing sledges were heavy wooden boards studded underneath with sharp stones or iron, dragged over grain; to thresh Gilead with them is to say a population was crushed like straw. The exile to Kir came true when Tiglath-pileser III took Damascus in 732 BC and deported its people.

Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron were four of the five Philistine cities. The fifth, Gath, is missing, perhaps because it had already been conquered. Gaza and Tyre sold whole communities to Edom, apparently as slaves for trade. Tyre's guilt is greater because it broke a covenant of brotherhood, probably a treaty with Israel like the one between Hiram and Solomon.
passages.later: Second Kings tells of Hazael's raids on Gilead (2 Kings 10:32-33) and of the exile to Kir: the king of Assyria captured Damascus, and ‘He took its people to Kir as captives’ (2 Kings 16:9). Hiram and Solomon made a treaty (1 Kings 5:12).
passages.asks: Amos begins with other nations' crimes, and his hearers would have nodded along. Ask how easily you agree when someone else's sin is named. And ask who in your world is being handed over and sold, and whether you notice.

passages.happening:
Edom is judged ‘because he pursued his brother with the sword and stifled all compassion’ (verse 11). His anger raged without end. So God will send fire on Teman to consume the citadels of Bozrah (verse 12).

The Ammonites are judged for a war crime against the pregnant women of Gilead, committed ‘in order to enlarge their territory’ (verse 13). These notes name it and do not describe it. God will kindle a fire in the walls of Rabbah amid the shouts of battle and a storm, and their king and his princes will go into exile together (verses 14-15).
passages.hearers:
Edom lay south of the Dead Sea, and its towns Teman and Bozrah stand for the whole country. Edom and Israel came from the brothers Esau and Jacob, so Edom's pursuit of his brother with the sword is a betrayal of kinship. Ammon lay east of the Jordan, with its capital at Rabbah, the site of modern Amman.

The crime of Ammon is among the most horrifying acts the Old Testament records. It was done for land. Amos names it so that no one can call it anything other than what it is.

The nations are arranged around Israel like a circle on a map, and the circle is closing. A hearer in Bethel would have agreed with every word so far. Chapter 2 turns the same judgment on Judah and then on Israel.
passages.later: Edom's descent from Esau, Jacob's brother, is told in Genesis 36:1. Obadiah gives a whole book to Edom's violence against his brother Jacob (Obadiah 10).
passages.hard:
How can God judge nations that never received his law?

Amos never accuses these nations of breaking the law of Moses or of failing to worship the LORD. Every charge is a crime against people: mass brutality, slave trading, broken treaties, relentless vengeance, the killing of the defenseless. The assumption is that some wrongs are known to be wrong by every people, whatever their religion or law. Many interpreters connect this with the covenant God made with all humanity through Noah, which forbids the shedding of human blood (Genesis 9:5-6). Others point to the treaties and customs of war of the ancient world itself, which these nations broke. Either way, Amos's God judges the nations by a standard they already knew, and he judges Israel, as chapter 2 shows, by the fuller standard it had been given.

These crimes are named in Scripture as crimes. They are named here and not described.
passages.asks: God holds every nation to account for cruelty, whether or not it knows his name. Ask what that says about how God sees the people others treat as expendable. And ask whether any ambition of yours, like Ammon's hunger for land, has made you blind to who gets hurt.
